Supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias
Amiodarone is used in the treatment of arrhythmias, particularly when other drugs are ineffective or contra-indicated. It can be used for
paroxysmal supraventricular, nodal and ventricular tachycardias, atrial fibrillation and flutter, and ventricular fibrillation. It can also be used for
tachyarrhythmias associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. It should be initiated only under hospital or specialist supervision.
Amiodarone may be given by intravenous infusion as well as by mouth. Intravenous amiodarone acts relatively rapidly, compared with oral
amiodarone; however, myocardial depression can occur with intravenous administration. Oral therapy has the advantage of causing minimal, if
any, myocardial depression.
Intravenous injection of amiodarone can be used in cardiopulmonary resuscitation for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless tachycardia
unresponsive to other interventions (see Cardiopulmonary resuscitation).

Peak flow meters
When used in addition to symptom-based monitoring, peak flow monitoring has not been proven to improve asthma control in either adults or
children, however measurement of peak flow may occasionally be of benefit for adult patients who are ‘poor perceivers’ and hence slow to detect
deterioration in their asthma, and for those with more severe asthma.
Patients should receive a clear written and verbal action plan of what action they should take if self-monitored peak flow falls below a certain
level. Patients can be encouraged to adjust some of their own treatment (within specified limits) according to changes in peak flow rate.

Antidiuretic hormone antagonists
Demeclocycline [section 29, unapproved medicine] (section 5.1.3) can be used in the treatment of hyponatraemia resulting from inappropriate
secretion of antidiuretic hormone, if fluid restriction alone does not restore sodium concentration or is not tolerable. Demeclocycline is thought to
act by directly blocking the renal tubular effect of antidiuretic hormone. Initially 0.9–1.2 g is given daily in divided doses, reduced to 600–900 mg
daily for maintenance.
Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist, there are two formulations available for different indications.
Jinarc® is used in the management of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with renal impairment to slow progression of cyst
formation and renal insufficiency. Long-term treatment requires careful monitoring of fluid, electrolytes, and hepatic function to avoid dehydration
and potentially serious liver injury.
Samsca® [section 29, unapproved medicine] is used for the treatment of hyponatraemia secondary to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic
hormone secretion; treatment duration is determined by the underlying disease and its treatment. Rapid correction of hyponatraemia
during therapy can cause osmotic demyelination, leading to serious neurological events; close monitoring of serum sodium concentration and
hydration status is essential.

Tetracyclines are active against a wide range of pathogens, particularly respiratory pathogens and chlamydia. They have anti-inflammatory
effects making them useful for dermatological indications such as acne, rosacea, and perioral dermatitis. As tetracyclines are bacteriostatic,
some conditions may require weeks or months of treatment. For further information see Acne and rosacea and Systemic antibiotics.

Extemporaneous preparations
 Extemporaneously compounded medicines may be useful when a required dose or dose form is unavailable commercially, or for individualised
dosing. For example, compounding may be useful for a patient with dysphagia where the only proprietary product available is a solid dosage
form.
Active pharmaceutical ingredients can be incorporated into a wide array of products including creams, eye drops, nasal sprays, and oral liquids.
Unlike approved, commercially available medicines, extemporaneously compounded preparations have generally not been assessed for safety
and efficacy. Compounding oral liquids is associated with potential risks including chemical and physical instability, inaccurate dosage (including
possible overdosage), and medication error—see Safety Alert - Caution Required with Compounded Oral Liquid Formulations Pharmacy
Council, April 2019. The NZ Compounding Working Group (CWG) have also developed General guidance for compounding oral liquids.

15.1.5 Neuromuscular blocking drugs
  Important
  The drugs in this section should only be administered by, or under direct supervision of, personnel experienced in their use, with adequate
  training in anaesthesia and airway management.

Neuromuscular blocking drugs used in anaesthesia are also known as muscle relaxants. By specifically blocking the neuromuscular junction
they enable light anaesthesia to be used with adequate relaxation of the muscles of the abdomen and diaphragm. They also relax the vocal cords
and allow the passage of a tracheal tube. Their action differs from the muscle relaxants used in musculoskeletal disorders (section 10.2.2) that
act on the spinal cord or brain.

Diabetes monitoring
Blood-glucose monitoring using a meter gives a direct measure of the glucose concentration in blood at the time of the test and can detect
hypoglycaemia as well as hyperglycaemia. Individuals should be properly trained in the use of blood-glucose monitoring systems and the
appropriate action to take on the results obtained. Inadequate understanding of the normal fluctuations in blood-glucose can lead to confusion
and inappropriate action.
Individuals using multiple injection regimens should understand how to adjust their insulin dose according to their carbohydrate intake. With fixed-
dose insulin regimens carbohydrate intake needs to be regulated and should be distributed throughout the day to match the insulin regimen.
Self-monitoring of blood-glucose concentration is an integral part of disease management for all individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus. For
people with type 2 diabetes mellitus self-monitoring of blood-glucose concentration is recommended for those treated with insulin, at risk of
hypoglycaemia (e.g. on a sulfonylurea, or when fasting such as during Ramadan), during times when glycaemic control may be unstable or
changing (e.g. with changes in lifestyle, medications, when feeling unwell or during intercurrent illness), and during pregnancy. Monitoring of
blood-glucose levels can be a useful tool to help educate individuals about blood-glucose

▶ pralidoxime salts


pralidoxime salts
( pralidoxime chloride ; pralidoxime iodide ; pralidoxime methyliodide ; pralidoxime mesilate ; pralidoxime metilsulfate ; 2-PAM )
[section 29, unapproved medicine]

Drug action
Pralidoxime is a cholinesterase enzyme reactivator that acts mainly at the neuromuscular junction. If given within 24 hours of organophosphate
exposure it restores the function of acetylcholinesterase by cleaving the phosphate-ester bond between the organophosphate and
acetylcholinesterase. The restoration of acetylcholine breakdown reverses respiratory and skeletal muscle paralysis.

Indications
adjunct to atropine in the treatment of poisoning by an organophosphate

Gonadorelin analogues
Administration of gonadorelin analogues produces an initial phase of stimulation; continued administration is followed by down-regulation of
gonadotrophin-releasing hormone receptors, thereby reducing the release of gonadotrophins (follicle stimulating hormone and luteinising
hormone) which in turn leads to inhibition of androgen and estrogen production.
Gonadorelin analogues are used in the treatment of endometriosis, precocious puberty, infertility, male hypersexuality with severe sexual
deviation, anaemia due to uterine fibroids (together with iron supplementation), breast and prostate cancer (see Gonadorelin analogues) and
before intra-uterine surgery. Use of leuprorelin for three to four months before surgery reduces the uterine volume, fibroid size, and associated
bleeding; for women undergoing hysterectomy or myomectomy, a vaginal procedure is made more feasible following the use of a gonadorelin
analogue.

9.3 Intravenous nutrition
When adequate feeding through the alimentary tract is not possible, nutrients may be given by intravenous infusion. Parenteral nutrition may be
the sole source of nutrition (total parenteral nutrition), or the parenteral nutrition (PN) may be supplementary in addition to ordinary oral or tube
feeding (dual feeding). Complete enteral starvation is undesirable, and total PN is a last resort. Indications for PN include severe or prolonged
disorders of the gastro-intestinal tract (e.g. post-operative ileus, small bowel obstruction, enterocutaneous fistula, anastamotic leak), major
surgery, trauma and burns.
Parenteral nutrition requires the use of a solution containing nitrogen (as amino acids), glucose (carbohydrate), lipid, electrolytes, trace elements,
and vitamins. Parenteral nutrition is commonly provided by a pharmacy-based sterile production service in the form of a 2-litre dual chamber bag
with a clear phase (amino acids, glucose, electrolytes, trace elements, and water soluble vitamins) and a lipid emulsion phase (lipid and lipid-
soluble vitamins). Separation of the phases prolongs the shelf-life of the product; the phases are mixed in the closed sterile container system
immediately prior to use. Additives, including medicines, should not be mixed with PN solutions unless compatibility is known.
If the patient is able to take small amounts by mouth, vitamins may be given orally instead of via the PN solutions. Weekly or twice weekly
injections of Vitamin K may be required if it is not included in PN solutions.
The nutrition solution is preferably infused via a dedicated line of a central venous catheter that has been inserted under full surgical precautions.

2.7.2 Vasoconstrictor sympathomimetics
Vasoconstrictor sympathomimetics raise blood pressure by acting on alpha-adrenergic receptors to constrict peripheral vessels. Ephedrine,
metaraminol, noradrenaline, and phenylephrine are sometimes used as an emergency method of elevating blood pressure when other
measures have failed (see also Inotropic sympathomimetics). Midodrine, an orally administered prodrug of desglymidodrine, may be useful for
neuropathic postural hypotension or hypotension secondary to medical conditions (e.g. diabetes, Parkinson’s disease) if other measures are
inadequate.
The danger of vasoconstrictors is that although they raise blood pressure they also reduce perfusion of vital organs such as the kidney.
Spinal and epidural anaesthesia may result in sympathetic block and resultant hypotension. Management may include intravenous fluids (which
are usually given prophylactically), oxygen, elevation of the legs, and injection of a pressor drug such as ephedrine. Ephedrine is a peripheral
vasoconstrictor that also increases heart rate and cardiac output via action on the beta-adrenoreceptors, which is useful if bradycardia occurs. If
bradycardia persists, atropine may be used.

8.1.1 Alkylating drugs
Extensive experience is available with these drugs, which are among the most widely used in cancer chemotherapy. They act by damaging
DNA, thus interfering with cell replication. In addition to the adverse effects common to many cytotoxic drugs (section 8.1), there are two
problems associated with prolonged usage. Firstly, gametogenesis is often severely affected (section 8.1). Secondly, prolonged use of these
drugs, particularly when combined with extensive irradiation, is associated with a marked increase in the incidence of acute non-lymphocytic
leukaemia.
Cyclophosphamide is used mainly in combination with other agents for treating a wide range of malignancies, including some leukaemias,
lymphomas, and solid tumours. It is given by mouth or intravenously; it is inactive until metabolised by the liver. A urinary metabolite of

intravenous injection, can prevent this complication. When high-dose therapy (e.g. more than 2 g intravenously) is used or when the patient is

 8.1.3 Antimetabolites
Antimetabolites are incorporated into new nuclear material or combine irreversibly with cellular enzymes, preventing normal cellular division.
Methotrexate inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase, essential for the synthesis of purines and pyrimidines. It is given by mouth,
intravenously, intramuscularly, or intrathecally.
Methotrexate is used as maintenance therapy for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Other uses include choriocarcinoma, non-Hodgkin's
lymphoma, and a number of solid tumours. Intrathecal methotrexate is used in the CNS prophylaxis of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia,
and as a therapy for established meningeal cancer or lymphoma.
Methotrexate causes myelosuppression, mucositis, and rarely pneumonitis. It is contra-indicated in significant renal impairment because it is
excreted primarily by the kidney. It is also contra-indicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment. It should also be avoided in the presence
of significant pleural effusion or ascites because it can accumulate in these fluids, and its subsequent return to the circulation may cause
myelosuppression. Systemic toxicity may follow intrathecal administration and blood counts should be carefully monitored.
Folinic acid (section 8.1) following methotrexate administration helps to prevent methotrexate-induced mucositis or myelosuppression.
Fluorouracil and capecitabine are fluoropyrimidines. Fluorouracil (or 5FU), a pyrimidine analogue, is given intravenously; capecitabine is an
oral prodrug of fluorouracil. Fluoropyrimidines are used to treat a number of solid tumours, including gastro-intestinal tract cancers, and breast

12.3.1 Drugs for oral ulceration and inflammation
Ulceration of the oral mucosa may be caused by trauma (physical or chemical), recurrent aphthae, infections, carcinoma, dermatological
disorders, nutritional deficiencies, gastro-intestinal disease, haematopoietic disorders, and drug therapy (see also Chemotherapy-induced
mucositis and myelosuppression, section 8.1). It is important to establish the diagnosis in each case as the majority of these lesions require
specific management in addition to local treatment. Local treatment aims to protect the ulcerated area, to relieve pain, to reduce inflammation, or
to control secondary infection. Patients with an unexplained mouth ulcer of more than 3 weeks' duration require urgent referral to hospital to
exclude oral cancer.

Simple mouthwashes
A saline mouthwash may relieve the pain of traumatic ulceration. The mouthwash is made up with warm water and used at frequent intervals
until the discomfort and swelling subsides.

Antiseptic mouthwashes
Secondary bacterial infection may be a feature of any mucosal ulceration; it can increase discomfort and delay healing. Use of chlorhexidine
mouthwash (section 12.3.4) is often beneficial and may accelerate healing of recurrent aphthae.

Mechanical protection
Carmellose sodium and pectin paste (Orabase®) may relieve some discomfort arising from ulceration by protecting the ulcer site. As the paste
adheres to dry mucosa, it is difficult to apply to the tongue and oropharynx.

Niraparib and olaparib are poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. PARP enzymes are involved in repair of single-strand DNA breaks.

 Parkinson's disease
In idiopathic Parkinson's disease, the progressive degeneration of pigmented neurones in the substantia nigra leads to a deficiency of the
neurotransmitter dopamine. The resulting neurochemical imbalance in the basal ganglia causes the characteristic signs and symptoms of the
illness. Drug therapy does not prevent disease progression, but it improves most patients' quality of life.
Patients with suspected Parkinson's disease should be referred to a specialist to confirm the diagnosis; the management should be reviewed
every 6–12 months.
Features resembling those of Parkinson's disease can occur in diseases such as progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy and
corticobasal syndrome, but they do not normally show a sustained response to the drugs used in the treatment of idiopathic Parkinson's
disease.
When initiating treatment, patients should be advised about its limitations and possible adverse effects. About 5–10% of patients with Parkinson's
disease respond poorly to treatment.
Treatment is usually not started until symptoms cause some disruption of daily life. Levodopa, non-ergot-derived dopamine-receptor
agonists, monoamine-oxidase-B inhibitors or antimuscarinics can be prescribed for initial treatment in early Parkinson's disease. Therapy
with two or more antiparkinsonian drugs may be necessary as the disease progresses. Most patients eventually r

15.1.4.3 Opioid analgesics
Opioid analgesics are now rarely used as premedicants; they are more likely to be administered at induction. Pre-operative use of opioid
analgesics is generally limited to those patients who require control of existing pain. The main adverse effects of opioid analgesics are
respiratory depression, cardiovascular depression, nausea, and vomiting; for general notes on opioid analgesics and their use in post-operative
pain, see section 4.7.2.
For the management of opioid-induced respiratory depression, see section 15.1.7.

Intra-operative analgesia
Opioid analgesics given in small doses before or with induction reduce the dose requirement of some drugs used during anaesthesia.
Alfentanil, fentanyl, and remifentanil are particularly useful because they act within 1–2 minutes and have short durations of action. The initial
doses of alfentanil or fentanyl are followed either by successive intravenous injections or by an intravenous infusion; prolonged infusions increase
the duration of effect. Repeated intra-operative doses of alfentanil or fentanyl should be given with care since the resulting respiratory depression
 can persist post-operatively. Occasionally it may become apparent for the first time post-operatively when monitoring of the patient might be less
intensive. Alfentanil, fentanyl, and remifentanil can cause muscle rigidity, particularly of the chest wall or jaw; this can be managed by the use of
neuromuscular blocking drugs (section 15.1.5).

 1.8.4 Anal fissures
Description of condition
An anal fissure is a tear or ulcer in the lining of the anal canal that can be intensely painful. Most anal fissures are caused by straining during
bowel movements, constipation or repeated diarrhoea. Clinical features of anal fissure include bleeding, persistent pain on defecation, and a
linear split in the anal mucosa. Spontaneous resolution occurs in one third of cases and usually within 6 weeks. Anal fissures that persist are
considered chronic and are managed more intensively.

Aims of treatment
The aim of treatment is to relieve pain and promote healing of the fissure.

Drug treatment

Acute anal fissure
Initial management of acute anal fissures (present for less than 6 weeks) involves lifestyle changes and symptomatic relief. Increasing dietary
fibre in the form of bran or use of a bulk-forming laxative (see Bulk-forming laxatives) is recommended to soften stools so that they are easily
passed; an osmotic laxative (such as lactulose or macrogol) may be considered as an alternative—see also Constipation. Short-term use of a
topical preparation containing a local anaesthetic (such as lidocaine hydrochloride) or a simple analgesic (such as paracetamol or ibuprofen)
may be offered for prolonged burning pain following defecation.

Chronic anal fissure
Anal fissures usually heal in three to six weeks, those that don't heal require further treatment measures. Following three weeks of conservative
treatment, anal fissures and associated pain can be treated with glyceryl trinitrate rectal ointment 0.2%. Treatment should be continued for at

Anticholinesterases are used as first-line treatment in ocular myasthenia gravis and as an adjunct to immunosuppressant therapy for

Anticholinesterases
Anticholinesterase drugs enhance neuromuscular transmission in voluntary and involuntary muscle in myasthenia gravis. They prolong the
action of acetylcholine by inhibiting the action of the enzyme acetylcholinesterase. Excessive dosage of these drugs can impair neuromuscular
transmission and precipitate cholinergic crises by causing a depolarising block. This may be difficult to distinguish from a worsening myasthenic
state.

 9.6.2 Vitamin B group
Deficiency of the B vitamins, other than vitamin B12 (see Drugs used in megaloblastic anaemias), is rare in New Zealand and is usually treated
by preparations containing thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), and nicotinamide, which is used in preference to nicotinic acid, as it does not cause
vasodilation. Other members (or substances traditionally classified as members) of the vitamin B complex such as aminobenzoic acid, biotin,
 choline, inositol, and pantothenic acid or panthenol may be included in vitamin B preparations but there is no evidence of their value.
The severe deficiency states Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, especially as seen in chronic alcoholism, are best treated
initially by parenteral administration of thiamine alone or as Pabrinex® (thiamine in combination with vitamins B2, B3, B6, and C) [both section
29, unapproved medicines], followed by thiamine in the longer term. Administration of glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen
Wernicke's encephalopathy; thiamine should be administered before glucose. Anaphylaxis has been reported occasionally with parenteral B
vitamins; patients should be monitored during and following administration and resuscitation facilities should be available.

Cardiovascular disease risk assessment and management
Description of the condition
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a collective term describing a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels caused by atherosclerosis and
thrombosis. The term includes conditions such as ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, stroke,
peripheral arterial disease, and aortic disease.
 The risk of acquired cardiovascular disease increases with advancing age, is higher in those with family history of cardiovascular disease,
severe psychiatric illness, chronic kidney disease and in certain ethnic backgrounds including Māori, Pacific and South Asian (i.e. Indian,
including Fijian Indian, Sri Lankan, Afghani, Bangladeshi, Nepalese, Pakistani, Tibetan) populations. Although women share similar risks for

8.3 Sex hormones and hormone antagonists in malignant disease
Hormonal manipulation with endocrine therapy (hormone therapy) has an important role in the treatment of breast, prostate, endometrial, and
endocrine cancers. It has a more marginal role in the treatment of renal cell carcinoma. In early-stage breast cancer, endocrine therapy is an
important component of adjuvant treatment. In advanced or metastatic hormone-sensitive breast cancer these treatments are not curative, but
can prolong life, delay time until deterioration in quality of life, and provide palliation of symptoms sometimes for years. Hormone therapy of
prostate cancer includes anti-androgen therapy to block the effects of androgens, or androgen deprivation therapy either medically using a
gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist (reduces androgen levels), or surgically with a bilateral orchidectomy (removes the
endogenous supply of androgens).
Hormonal manipulation may be used alone or in conjunction with other treatments such as targeted treatments, e.g. used with CDK4/6 inhibitors
in the initial treatment of advanced breast cancer.
 Tumour response and treatment toxicity should be carefully monitored, and treatment changed if progression occurs, or adverse effects
outweigh benefit.

Opioid reversal
Respiratory depression is a major concern with opioid analgesics and may be treated by artificial ventilation or be reversed by an opioid
antagonist. Naloxone given intravenously immediately reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression. Intramuscular naloxone produces a more
gradual and prolonged effect but absorption may be erratic. Subcutaneous administration also has a slower onset. A nasal spray is available for

Eribulin mesilate is a non-taxane microtubule inhibitor. It is indicated for locally-advanced or metastatic breast cancer, following progression
after treatment for advanced disease, and for unresectable liposarcoma in individuals who have received prior chemotherapy for advanced or
metastatic disease. Eribulin mesilate can cause peripheral neuropathy and patients should be carefully monitored for symptoms. Other common
adverse effects include neutropenia and fatigue. QT prolongation has been reported, electrolytes should be assessed and corrected prior to
initiating treatment.

eribulin mesilate
Drug action
Eribulin, a synthetic analogue of halichondrin B, is a non-taxane microtubule inhibitor. It inhibits the growth phase of microtubules and sequesters
tubulin into non-productive aggregates disrupting formation of mitotic spindles. This halts cell division and leads to apoptotic cell death. It is
specific for the G2/M phase of the cell-cycle.

8.1.2 Anthracyclines and other cytotoxic antibiotics
Drugs in this group are widely used. Many cytotoxic antibiotics act as radiomimetics and simultaneous use of radiotherapy should be avoided
because it may markedly increase toxicity.
Daunorubicin, doxorubicin, epirubicin, and idarubicin are anthracycline antibiotics. Mitoxantrone is an anthracycline derivative.

dosage and administration, and are not interchangeable. Conventional doxorubicin is used to treat the acute leukaemias, Hodgkin's and non-

5.1.4 Aminoglycosides
These include amikacin, gentamicin, neomycin and tobramycin. All are bactericidal and active against some Gram-positive and many Gram-
negative organisms. Amikacin, gentamicin, and tobramycin are also active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Streptomycin [section 29,
unapproved medicine] is another aminoglycoside, it is active against Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is now almost entirely reserved for
tuberculosis (section 5.1.9).
The aminoglycosides are not absorbed from the gastro-intestinal tract (although there is a risk of absorption in inflammatory bowel disease and
liver failure) and must therefore be given by injection for systemic infections.
The important adverse effects of aminoglycosides are ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; they occur most commonly in the elderly and in patients
with renal failure.
Gentamicin is the aminoglycoside of choice in New Zealand and is used widely for the treatment of serious infections. It has a broad spectrum
but is inactive against anaerobes and has poor activity against haemolytic streptococci and pneumococci. When used for the empiric therapy of
undiagnosed serious infections it is usually given in conjunction with a penicillin, metronidazole, or both. Gentamicin is used for synergistic effect
with other antibiotics in the treatment of endocarditis.
Loading and maintenance doses of gentamicin may be calculated using the individual's ideal body weight and renal function; adjustments are
then made according to serum-gentamicin concentrations. High doses may be indicated for serious infections, in those with cystic fibrosis, or in
immunocompromised individuals. Courses longer than five
